newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish peace quest reopens, clouded by violence.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish peace quest reopens, clouded by violence.

text.p: Britain renewed a call to the IRA on Tuesday to announce a lasting ceasefire so that its political wing can take part in talks, as fresh discussions to nurse Northern Ireland's ailing peace process to life were set to start.
Mo Mowlam, Northern Ireland Secretary in Britain's newly-elected Labour government, ruled out a talks seat for Sinn Fein while its Irish Republican Army ally was on a war footing.

She dismissed a suggestion that hopes of a truce had evaporated. "No, I don't accept that at all. We (Labour) have only been going for three weeks. We will still try and get the talks inclusive," she said on BBC radio.
"We would prefer to have Sinn Fein around the table rather than not but that is dependent on a meaningful ceasefire, an unequivocal ceasefire with supporting words and deeds."
Britain, backed by Ireland, says no party at the table can have a private army lurking in the background.

The talks, which first started a year ago, were adjourned during British national elections, which returned a Labour government after 18 years of Conservative rule and raised hopes of a breakthrough in the bitter conflict over British rule of Northern Ireland.

Emboldened by a rise in support among minority Catholic voters, the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm will make a largely symbolic but doomed bid to get into the talks that are due to resume at 2 p.m. (1300 GMT) in an office complex near Belfast.

Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams, elected along with a senior colleague as abstentionist members of the British parliament in the May 1 election, said his party had a right to take part in the talks which involve the province's other majority parties.
"I am not going up (to the talks) to demand anything other than the rights of those people who voted for us," he told reporters.

A six week IRA lull that helped create a climate for recently resumed low-level "clarification talks" between Sinn Fein and Britain ended in a 500 kg (1,100 pound) bomb scare in Belfast over the weekend.
Police found the explosives in a burnt-out van and said the IRA had tried to ensnare them into a trap.
Security forces said on Tuesday they could find no trace of an anti-personnel mine that the IRA, in a coded call to a radio station, said they left overnight near a Belfast army base.

Pro-British Protestant hardliners, in the runup to what is feared will be a turbulent period of parades through Catholic zones, were blamed on Sunday for the mob killing of a police officer, who was kicked to death.
"Loyalist" militias, pledged to thwart the IRA's aim of ending British rule, have shot dead two Catholic nationalists in the past year and injured others in booby-trap bomb attacks.

Tuesday's talks are expected to restart with a short round-table session and then return to a pattern of bilateral discussions between the Protestant and Catholic parties and the British and Irish governments.
Overshadowed by resurgent guerrilla activity, the talks have struggled to make any progress.

Politicians spent the first months arguing over procedures and were then embroiled in unresolved disputes over the terms for Sinn Fein's entry and how to achieve disarmament by the rival guerrilla groups.

Protestant parties speaking for the province's pro-British majority say the IRA must hand in arms before Sinn Fein gets a seat. Sinn Fein accuses Britain of double-standards for giving Loyalist parties seats despite Loyalist violence.

Moderate Catholics, who want an IRA truce, say London and Dublin must urgently steer the talks towards wide-ranging political issues and not allow the vexed issue of "arms decommissioning" to hold up progress any longer.
Talks chairman former U.S.senator George Mitchell said the riven community yearns for calm but added that he did not underestimate the obstacles.
"I believe that the opportunity exists for substantial and substantive progress to be made in these talks, that's why I've come back," he told reporters in Belfast.
